questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex set and $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$. Which condition defines $f$ to be quasi-convex?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\geq\alpha\}$ is convex for every $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ is convex for some $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$ is convex for every $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})=\alpha\}$ is convex for every $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex and $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$. Which inequality, required for all $\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}\in D$ and all $\lambda\in[0,1]$, is equivalent to $f$ being quasi-convex?
options: $f(\lambda\boldsymbol{a}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{b})\leq\lambda f(\boldsymbol{a})+(1-\lambda)f(\boldsymbol{b})$
$f(\lambda\boldsymbol{a}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{b})\leq\max\{f(\boldsymbol{a}),f(\boldsymbol{b})\}$
$f(\lambda\boldsymbol{a}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{b})\geq\min\{f(\boldsymbol{a}),f(\boldsymbol{b})\}$
$f(\lambda\boldsymbol{a}+(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{b})\leq\min\{f(\boldsymbol{a}),f(\boldsymbol{b})\}$

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex. Which statement about the relation between convex and quasi-convex functions $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ is correct?
options: Every convex function is quasi-convex, and the converse fails.
Every quasi-convex function is convex, and the converse fails.
The two classes coincide, since both have convex sublevel sets.
A quasi-convex function is convex as soon as it is continuous.

questions.question: Let $f$ be quasi-convex on the open interval $(-1,1)$. Which statement about the continuity of $f$ is correct?
options: $f$ is continuous on $(-1,1)$, as every convex function on an open interval is.
$f$ is continuous on $(-1,1)$, because each sublevel set of $f$ is an interval.
$f$ is continuous at every point near which it is strictly increasing.
$f$ can be discontinuous at an interior point, as a step function shows.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing, with no further assumption. Which statement about whether $f$ is quasi-convex is correct?
options: $f$ is quasi-convex only if it is continuous; a jump leaves a gap in a sublevel set.
$f$ is quasi-convex only if it is also convex, so $x^3$ is excluded.
$f$ is quasi-convex: if $a<z<b$, then $f(z)\leq f(b)=\max\{f(a),f(b)\}$.
$f$ is quasi-convex only if it is strictly increasing, so flat pieces are excluded.

questions.question: For $f(x)=\ln(1+x^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, which set is the sublevel set $L_{\ln 10}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon f(x)\leq\ln 10\}$?
options: $(-\infty,-3]\cup[3,\infty)$

questions.question: Let $f(\boldsymbol{x})=(x_1+2x_2)^3$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which description of the set of all points $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq8$ is correct?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\leq8\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\geq2\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon -2\leq x_1+2x_2\leq2\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\leq2\}$

questions.question: Let $f(x)=1$ for $|x|\leq1$ and $f(x)=0$ for $|x|>1$, on $\mathbb{R}$. Test $f(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b)\leq\max\{f(a),f(b)\}$ with $a=-2$, $b=2$, $\lambda=\tfrac{1}{2}$. What does this check show about whether $f$ is quasi-convex?
options: $f(0)=1>0$, so $f$ is not convex, but $f$ may still be quasi-convex.
$f(0)=1>0=\max\{f(-2),f(2)\}$, so $f$ is not quasi-convex.
$f$ is quasi-convex anyway, since it has no strict local maximum.
Nothing follows yet, since only one value of $\lambda$ was checked.

questions.question: Let $M(x)=\max\{x^3,\,-2x\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Which set is the sublevel set $\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon M(x)\leq8\}$?
options: $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: Which of the following functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is not quasi-convex?
options: $f(x)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-x}$

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ and, for $\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^2$, let $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}}(t)=f(\boldsymbol{a}+t(\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{a}))$ for $t\in[0,1]$, the values of $f$ along the segment from $\boldsymbol{a}$ to $\boldsymbol{b}$. Which condition is equivalent to $f$ being quasi-convex?
options: For every $c\in\mathbb{R}$, the functions $x_1\mapsto f(x_1,c)$ and $x_2\mapsto f(c,x_2)$ are quasi-convex.
For all $\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^2$, the function $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}}$ is quasi-convex on $[0,1]$.
For all $\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^2$, the function $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}}$ is monotone on $[0,1]$.
For all $\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^2$, the function $\varphi_{\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}}$ is convex on $[0,1]$.

questions.question: The definition of a quasi-convex function $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ requires the domain $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ to be convex. Why is this requirement needed?
options: Otherwise a segment between points of $D$ may leave $D$, where $f$ is undefined.
Otherwise $f$ could be discontinuous, and the definition relies on continuity.
Otherwise some sublevel set could be empty, and the empty set is not convex.
Otherwise sublevel sets could fail to be closed, and convex sets must be closed.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be quasi-convex. Which statement about local maxima of $f$ is correct?
options: $f$ has no local maximum anywhere, since any local maximum violates the max-inequality.
$f$ can have a strict local maximum, provided $f$ is continuous at that point.
$f$ can have a strict local maximum, but only at a point where $f$ is discontinuous.
$f$ can have a local maximum, but not a strict local maximum.

questions.question: Let $m(x)=\min\{x^2,(x-4)^2\}$ on $\mathbb{R}$; both $x^2$ and $(x-4)^2$ are convex. Which statement about $\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon m(x)\leq1\}$ and quasi-convexity of $m$ is correct?
options: It equals $[-1,1]\cap[3,5]=\varnothing$, which is convex, so $m$ is quasi-convex.
It equals $[-1,5]$, which is convex, so $m$ is quasi-convex.
It equals $[-1,1]\cup[3,5]$, which is not convex, so $m$ is not quasi-convex.
It equals $[-1,1]\cup[3,5]$, but $m$ is quasi-convex as a minimum of convex functions.

questions.question: Let $f(\boldsymbol{x})=\sqrt{|x_1|+|x_2|}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, with sublevel sets $L_{\alpha}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon f(\boldsymbol{x})\leq\alpha\}$. Which classification of $f$ is correct?
options: Quasi-convex but not convex: each $L_{\alpha}$ is convex, yet $f(0,2)>\tfrac{1}{2}(f(0,0)+f(0,4))$.
Convex: each $L_{\alpha}$ with $\alpha\geq0$ is the convex set $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon|x_1|+|x_2|\leq\alpha^2\}$.
Not quasi-convex: $f(0,2)=\sqrt{2}$ exceeds the average $1$ of $f(0,0)=0$ and $f(0,4)=2$.
Not quasi-convex: the sublevel set $L_{\alpha}$ is empty for every level $\alpha<0$.

questions.question: A quasi-convex function $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $f(1)=2$ and $f(5)=7$. Which set consists of exactly the values that $f(3)$ can take?
Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be quasi-convex with $f(0)<f(1)$. Which statement about $f$ is guaranteed?
options: $f$ is nondecreasing on the whole of $\mathbb{R}$.
$f(x)\geq f(0)$ holds for every $x\geq0$.
$f$ is nonincreasing on $(-\infty,0]$.
$f$ is nondecreasing on $[1,\infty)$.

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex, $f\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ quasi-convex and $g\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ nondecreasing. Which statement about the composition $g\circ f$ is correct?
options: $g\circ f$ is always quasi-convex, because $g$ preserves the max-inequality of $f$.
$g\circ f$ is quasi-convex only when $g$ is convex as well as nondecreasing.
$g\circ f$ is even convex whenever $f$ is convex, since $g$ preserves order.
$g\circ f$ is quasi-convex only when $g$ is strictly increasing, with no flat pieces.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^4-2x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$; its minimum value is $f(\pm1)=-1$ and $f(0)=0$. For which levels $\alpha$ is the sublevel set $\{x\in\mathbb{R}\colon f(x)\leq\alpha\}$ not convex?
options: $\alpha<0$
$-1\leq\alpha<0$
$-1\leq\alpha\leq0$

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}$ let $g(x)=0$ for $x\leq0$ and $g(x)=1$ for $x>0$, and $h(x)=1$ for $x<1$ and $h(x)=0$ for $x\geq1$. Which statement about $g$, $h$, $g+h$ and $\max\{g,h\}$ is correct?
options: $g+h$ is quasi-convex, as a sum of the two quasi-convex functions $g$ and $h$.
$g+h$ is not quasi-convex, since $\{g+h\leq1\}=(-\infty,0]\cup[1,\infty)$.
$g+h$ is not quasi-convex, and neither is the maximum $\max\{g,h\}$.
$h$ is not quasi-convex, since it is nonincreasing rather than nondecreasing.
